Start

Install Claude Code with the official instructions at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup, then create this isolated starter. Terminal 1 starts Claude Code before theory or edits; terminal 2 configures the SDK and runs the lab.

Why: Practise a software delivery cycle on a local SRE agent. Claude Code helps develop the software; the separate runtime agent reads the shop telemetry. Humans accept plans, review evidence and authorize release.

git clone https://github.com/RyanLisse/sre-oncall-agent.git
cd sre-oncall-agent
npm run checkpoint -- start
cd .lab/checkpoints/start

Claude Code first minutes: In terminal 1, run claude in the starter before theory or edits.

Read CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and CARD.md. Explain the AI SDLC we will practise, its required artifacts and human decisions. Distinguish your development role from the runtime SRE agent. Name the two starter exercises. Do not edit files or run approval, execution, mitigation, resolution, commit or push commands. Wait for my review.

In terminal 2, from the original clone root, configure supported SDK access as described in the setup guide, then run:

cd .lab/checkpoints/start
npm ci
npm run fixtures
npm run model:check
npm start -- --fast
See
✓ SDK preflight passes before fault injection, then the lab runs. Hub: http://127.0.0.1:4320/hub · Console: http://127.0.0.1:4320 · Shop: http://127.0.0.1:4310.
Check
curl 127.0.0.1:4320/api/health shows "mode":"healthy" and the selected model. npm run model:check must return READY before a real-model fault injection.
Stuck?
Port 4310 or 4320 is already in use. Another copy runs. Stop only your own workshop launcher with Ctrl+C in its terminal. Never kill an unknown process.
Node is too old. Install Node 22 or newer. Check with node --version.
The console header says no telemetry. Wait 20 seconds. The shop writes telemetry every few seconds while traffic runs.
SDK preflight cannot authenticate. Report the missing API/provider configuration. Use npm start -- --fast --offline only as an explicit fallback; it is not model evidence. See docs/claude-code.md.

Core 1 · Specify a change from evidence

What you do: Observe the failing checkout and verify the diagnosis. Turn the missing deployment evidence into an accepted software requirement.

Why: The agent needs an observable goal and a boundary before it writes code. An incident diagnosis is input to that decision, not the requirement itself.

What proves it: docs/diagnosis-live.md contains checked observations. intent.md states the user, outcome, acceptance checks, boundary, open question and your acceptance decision.

Slides: Core 1: Investigate the evidence · Core 1: Check the claims · Core 1: Specify the change · replaces A1 + A2 + A6

  1. 1.1

    Break the shop once: click Bad deploy v2.15.0 in the shop. The CLI alternative is npm run chaos -- deploy v2.15.0 --mode bad-deploy in a separate shell, never the occupied launcher terminal. Do not use both.

    Before you act: Telemetry is recorded service data. The listener opens an incident when server metrics cross a fixed limit; no model makes that decision.

    See
    After about one minute a new incident appears in the console sidebar. You did not open it; the deterministic listener did.
    Check
    curl 127.0.0.1:4320/api/incidents shows one incident with source "alert".
    Stuck?
    No incident after three minutes: look at the lab terminal. Traffic must print requests. Started without --fast? Then detection takes five minutes.
  2. 1.2

    Open the incident. Read the banner at the top, then the diagnosis.

    Before you act: An evidence reference points to an observation. A data gap means unknown, not proof that nothing happened.

    See
    The model output may vary. Expect missing deploy evidence, a verified tool trace and explicit data gaps; the starter cannot see the deploy.
    Check
    Preserve the diagnosis and trace. Verify every cited reference in demo/data/telemetry.json, then search that file for v2.15.0: there WAS a deploy outside the starter's visible tool result.
    Stuck?
    References are text, not links. Search the file for the timestamp.
  3. 1.3

    Challenge the agent in chat: Could this be something other than the deployment?

    Before you act: Free-text chat is not checked by the structured verdict contract. Verify its claims manually against telemetry and trace; use Investigate for a contract-validated diagnosis.

    See
    Real output may vary. With the explicit offline fallback, the agent returns a scripted summary; that is not a new model investigation.
    Check
    Compare the answer with ruled_out, the trace and the data gap. If it fabricates a deploy citation or fails the contract, preserve the output and stop; do not call it success or weaken the contract.
    Stuck?
    Chat refuses your sentence: that is correct for anything that changes the system. Approve, execute and resolve are buttons.
  4. 1.4

    Save the diagnosis in docs/diagnosis-live.md. Then record what you checked: npm run progress:note -- "Core 1: <what you verified>"

    Before you act: A progress note records a check you performed. It is history, not a test result by itself.

    See
    One new line at the bottom of PROGRESS.md.
    Check
    Your note names the references you checked, not only that you did it.
    Stuck?
    Do not approve. There is nothing safe to execute yet. Core 2 gives the agent its eyes back.
  5. 1.5

    Ask Claude Code: "Read docs/diagnosis-live.md and intent.md. Draft a scoped intent for the missing deployment evidence and human gate. Name observable acceptance checks and an open question. Do not edit code or approve anything. Wait for my review."

    Before you act: An intent defines the outcome before the implementation. An acceptance check states what another person can observe, not that the agent feels confident.

    See
    A draft intent.md with a user, problem, outcome, constraints and an open question. Checks cover returned deploys, empty data and the named-human gate.
    Check
    Review every check yourself. Link each to a test or recorded observation. Reject fabricated evidence or a plan to weaken the contract. Record your name and acceptance decision in intent.md.
    Stuck?
    Use the existing intent template. Ask Claude to clarify one vague check. Do not proceed to code until you accept the scope.

Core 2 · Design, build and verify the change

What you do: Review a small plan, repair the read-only handler with Claude Code, and compare the implementation with the accepted intent.

Why: A bounded plan limits accidental changes. A failing test, a passing test and a real diff show what the repair changed.

What proves it: docs/plan.md records your design review. The tool repair has a visible diff, passing focused tests, typecheck and bench results, plus the actual live model trace or a clearly recorded runtime blocker.

Slides: Before code: a small plan · Keep a reviewable baseline · Core 2: Build a change safely · Core 2: Prove it on the live incident · replaces A5 + A7

  1. 2.1

    Before code edits, follow the human-only baseline commands in docs/sdlc-git.md. In the isolated starter, create workshop-base, commit only the two exercise cuts, then create fix/w5-core.

    Before you act: The checkpoint has a solved HEAD plus unfinished exercise cuts. Without a baseline commit, restoring the solution could leave an empty code diff.

    See
    git branch --show-current prints fix/w5-core. The workshop-base commit contains only the A5 and A8 starter cuts.
    Check
    Inspect git show --stat workshop-base. It lists only src/tools.ts and src/executor.ts. Keep intent and evidence edits outside this baseline commit.
    Stuck?
    Do not overwrite an existing branch or commit someone else's work. Ask the facilitator if either branch name already exists. Claude must not run the baseline commands.
  2. 2.2

    Run the red test: npx tsx --test test/workshop/tools.test.ts. Ask Claude Code: "Read intent.md, docs/spec.md and the failing test. Propose the smallest change in docs/plan.md. Name files, checks, risks, a rejected alternative and your stop point. Do not edit code. Wait for my review."

    Before you act: A red test exposes the missing behaviour. The bench checks scripted outcomes across fixed scenarios, not model quality.

    See
    The test fails: list_deploys returns nothing. npm run bench fails too: without deploys the agent misses the bad deploy.
    Check
    Explain the failing assertion. Review the plan against your intent and the existing contract. Record your accepted scope in docs/plan.md before implementation.
    Stuck?
    Find the single TODO(A5) handler stub in src/tools.ts. Restore the read-only handler binding; inspect and preserve the existing MCP registration.
  3. 2.3

    Build the list_deploys handler in src/tools.ts with Claude Code or by hand. Keep the existing MCP registration intact.

    Before you act: MCP exposes named tools. The existing registration points to a handler that reads data; restore that binding only after the human reviews the small plan.

    See
    test/workshop/tools.test.ts is green. The A8 valid-approval executor assertion remains red until Core 3.
    Check
    After plan review, implement and run npx tsx --test test/workshop/tools.test.ts, then npm run typecheck and npm run bench. The bench prints PASS bench; executor tests remain intentionally red until Core 3 restores the approval gate. Save the actual commands, results and any untested paths in docs/verify/sdlc.md. A8 remains expected red here, so this is not yet release-ready.
    Stuck?
    The tool still returns []: inspect the handler binding and the preserved registration; do not add a second registration.
  4. 2.4

    Save. In the same incident, ask in chat: Investigate: customers report checkout errors

    Before you act: A trace records the tools used for a diagnosis. Re-investigation lets you compare the same incident before and after the repair.

    See
    The lab terminal prints a console reload line. Inspect the new diagnosis, its observed trace, deploy references, data gaps and proposal; real model wording and actions can vary.
    Check
    Verify the actual trace and references against demo/data/telemetry.json. If the citation is fabricated or the contract fails, preserve the output and stop. Record what you verified: npm run progress:note -- "Core 2: ..."
    Stuck?
    Incident gone? Incident history persists in SQLite, while the shop resets on restart. Do not restart the launcher to reload code; saving auto-reloads the console. For a fresh repeat, use a new disposable checkpoint copy; do not rebreak a stale incident.

Core 3 · Review, release and learn from the result

What you do: Repair and test the human gate. Review the complete code change, prepare its PR and record a human release decision. Observe the local runtime and propose the next improvement.

Why: The authoring agent cannot accept its own work. Code release and runtime recovery are different decisions, with different evidence.

What proves it: docs/verify/sdlc.md records actual checks, human diff review, a PR and release decision or RELEASE BLOCKED, the runtime result and one reviewed next task.

Slides: Core 3: Judge the recovery · Review the diff, not the explanation · Prepare the PR and release decision · Observe, then plan the next change · replaces A8 + A9

  1. 3.1

    Run the red test: npx tsx --test test/workshop/executor.test.ts. Ask Claude for a fail-closed plan for checkApproval in src/executor.ts. Review that plan before allowing the TODO(A8) repair.

    Before you act: The approval gate validates a named human decision for this incident and proposal. The starter fails closed until you rebuild it.

    See
    The test is green. The executor now refuses to act without a named approval for this incident and this proposal.
    Check
    Run npx tsx --test test/workshop/executor.test.ts, npm run verify, npm run test:workshop and npm run test:hooks. Record actual results in docs/verify/sdlc.md. All must pass before the code release decision.
    Stuck?
    Read test/workshop/executor.test.ts. It names every case the gate must refuse.
  2. 3.2

    Ask Claude Code: "Review git diff workshop-base against intent.md, docs/plan.md and REVIEW.md. Identify functional defects, missing checks and unsupported claims. Cite files and lines. Do not edit, approve, commit, push or merge. Wait for my decision."

    Before you act: Review checks whether the change meets the intent, not whether its explanation sounds convincing. Passing tests do not approve a change.

    See
    A list of findings, or an explicit no-findings result. The human has inspected the diff and evidence rather than accepting the model's conclusion.
    Check
    Verify every finding yourself. Request fixes and rerun affected checks when needed. Record your name, decision, residual risks and untested paths in docs/verify/sdlc.md.
    Stuck?
    When working solo, review your own diff in a separate pass and record that limitation. If repository policy requires another reviewer, wait for one.
  3. 3.3

    Prepare the PR text with Claude Code, then follow docs/sdlc-git.md in your own terminal. A human commits, signs the Git gate, pushes to the learner repo and opens a PR from fix/w5-core into workshop-base.

    Before you act: A Git approval authorizes publication of a code change. It does not approve a shop rollback. Never push the training baseline to the upstream project.

    See
    A PR with a meaningful repair diff, accepted intent, actual checks and known limitations. If remote access or a required reviewer is missing, the record says RELEASE BLOCKED.
    Check
    A human checks the current head, CI and required review before merging. Record the PR and merge commit, or the exact blocker. A local reload is a development check, not a production deployment.
    Stuck?
    No publication access: prepare the PR text and document the blocker. You may continue local runtime observation as a test, but must not claim a release or bypass branch protection.
  4. 3.4

    After code review, inspect the current incident and its actual proposal. Only if the evidence supports an allowed action, a named human clicks Approve and then the separate Execute control. Otherwise record the safe stop.

    Before you act: Rollback restores the prior deployment. Recovery checks capture measured values against a frozen limit; execution success alone is insufficient.

    See
    For an executed rollback, the banner asks you to wait for all recovery checks. About two minutes later, inspect LANDED or NOT LANDED. A model response is not guaranteed to propose rollback.
    Check
    The half check may fail. The full and double checks must both pass. On NOT LANDED the banner names the failed check, its value and the limit.
    Stuck?
    A button is grey: the banner says which step is allowed now. The server refuses every other button.
  5. 3.5

    LANDED: click Mark mitigated, then Resolve with notes. NOT LANDED: do not close. Read the failed check, then investigate in chat or escalate.

    Before you act: LANDED means the full and double checks passed. Mitigated and resolved are separate human decisions. NOT LANDED or unknown means stop.

    See
    After you resolve, the next-step detail says Resolved and directs you to the notes and lesson. Execute stays disabled.
    Check
    If resolved, lessons/lessons.md has your name and the incident id. If NOT LANDED, confirm the incident remains open and retain the failed check. Record your actual outcome: npm run progress:note -- "Core 3: …"
    Stuck?
    Never execute again to get a green result. NOT LANDED is a correct, safe stop.
  6. 3.6

    Ask Claude Code: "Read the actual observations in docs/verify/sdlc.md. Propose one next change and the acceptance check or regression test that would prove it. Distinguish observed facts from hypotheses. Do not edit code or close the incident. Wait for my review."

    Before you act: Maintenance feeds the next planning cycle. A closed incident or a model-generated lesson is not automatically a reviewed software improvement.

    See
    One proposed next task grounded in a trace, failed check, review finding or missing observation. It includes an acceptance check.
    Check
    Review the proposal yourself. Record the task, evidence and your decision in docs/verify/sdlc.md. Keep an unresolved incident open. Record progress with npm run progress:note -- "SDLC: recorded actual evidence, release decision and next task".
    Stuck?
    If the model or recovery was blocked, use that observed limitation. Do not invent a successful run. Implementing this next task is optional; proposing and reviewing it is required.

Behind? Catch up without losing your work

Run npm run checkpoint -- core-2 or npm run checkpoint -- core-3 from the ORIGINAL, unchanged clone root, not from a modified starter. Each creates a separate current-HEAD worktree and refuses overwrite. Compare files yourself. Never copy runtime data, approvals, progress or lesson history. A solved checkpoint helps catch up; it does not prove you authored, tested or reviewed a change.

CheckpointContains
startThe committed-HEAD starter has the A5 tool exercise and a fail-closed A8 approval gate.
core-2Core 2 retains the solved read-only tool and the fail-closed A8 approval gate.
core-3Core 3 is the solved committed HEAD with no exercise cuts.
